title: Fireside Tales of the Reach, Lately Told
author: Margery Fallow, who keeps the little school on Cooper's Row
summary: Three new tales told as if they were old, written down by a schoolmistress who noticed how quickly the children changed them.
text: I keep the little school on Cooper's Row. When the slates are put away and the hush-lamp is lit, we tell tales. I have written three of them down, because I noticed something about them and I want somebody after me to notice it too.

In every one of my grandmother's tales, the clever girl sang. She sang the wolves to sleep. She sang so loud that the miller heard her at Greenroot. The children will not have those tales now. If I tell one, a hand goes up: But Mistress, the hounds would come. So the tales have changed, and they have changed in about three years, and the children tell them back to me as if they were three hundred years old. Here they are as the children like them. I have only tidied the grammar.
CLEVER DORCAS AND THE JAR

There was a girl called Dorcas who lived on the far side of the water-meadow, back when there were people on the far side. Her mother sent her to her gran's for a jar of honey and told her to take the baby, because the baby would not settle for anyone else.

So Dorcas went over the meadow with the baby on her hip, and she came back with the honey in the good brown jar with the blue ring round its neck, which had been her gran's mother's. She was halfway home when the baby woke, saw the dark, and opened his mouth.

You know what a baby can do. He cried properly, a cry like a gate dragged over cobbles, and far off at the edge of the trees something heard it and turned. Dorcas saw the air go shivery there, the way it shakes over a summer road.

She could have clapped her hand over his mouth. But her gran had told her what becomes of babies who are made to go quiet in the dark, and Dorcas was not going to carry home a quiet baby. So she did a clever thing. She ate the honey. She ate all of it with two fingers, and never tasted a drop. Then she held the empty jar to the baby's mouth and let him cry into it, the whole cry, the long one. When he stopped to breathe, she pushed the stopper in.

She threw the jar as far as she could towards the Flume. It struck the stones by the bank and broke, and out of it came the baby's cry, every bit as loud as he had made it. The hounds went to the jar. Of course they did. They go where the loud thing is.

Then the baby, having cried himself empty, went still on her hip, and stiller, and she felt him getting cool. So she put her lips to the top of his head, where the bones are soft, and hummed into him: not loud, not quiet, the width of a hand. She walked home through the meadow humming, step for step, and the hounds were busy with the jar the whole way.

When she got in, her mother said, Where is the honey? Dorcas said, In me. Her mother said, Where is the jar? Dorcas said, Over by the Flume, with the hounds. Her mother sat down on the settle and laughed without making a sound, which Reach mothers can do, and then she cried the same way. Then she sent Dorcas to bed with no supper, which was fair, because Dorcas had had the honey.
And that is why, in the Reach, nobody will lend you a good jar. (The children insist on this ending. One of them tried to borrow mine afterwards.)
EBBO STINT, WHO ANSWERED

Ebbo Stint was the meanest man in Oakhaven, and in Oakhaven that is a contest. He had a wife called Tilda who did the kindness for both of them, and she died of it, the children say, though they say that about everybody. She was buried the proper way, with her jaw bound and a stone on her tongue. Then Ebbo went home to count his money, which she had always hidden for him, because he could never decide where. It was not where she had said. He turned the house inside out.
One night at the Hedge he heard her. Ebbo? Ebbo, love, are you warm enough?

Everyone knows you do not answer. Ebbo knew it better than anyone, because answering costs something, and he never paid for anything he could get free. So he walked past. For a month he walked past. She asked whether he was eating. She asked about the cat. She asked whether he had found the money yet, and he did not even slow down, though it nearly killed him.
Then one night she said, very sweetly: I put the thirty sovereigns under the hearthstone, love. You'll find them there.
Ebbo stopped dead in the lane. He turned to the thorn, and for the first time in his life he raised his voice. It was forty! There were forty!
In the morning there was his stick, leaning against the Hedge, as neat as if he had stood it there himself.

They lifted his hearthstone, of course. There was nothing under it. They took up the floor and the chimney, and to this day nobody has found Ebbo Stint's forty sovereigns. But if you walk along the Hedge behind the tannery of a night, and you are mean, and you are listening, you may hear a woman's voice say, very gently: Forty, love. It was forty.

The moral, the children tell me, is not to answer. I think the moral is that it did not know the number until he told it. That is the whole of the Hedge in one sentence, and I would rather they learned it from Ebbo than from anyone they love.
WHY THE OAKS RING

When the Synod's men came for the bells, the year the quarry opened, they took the six from the Chapel and the little wind-bells out of the reed-rows. They put them in a wagon under sacking and drove them up the quarry road to be made into teeth for the bore. Nobody said anything. By then everybody knew what bells bring.

But the oaks watched too. The oaks of Oakhaven are old, and they had heard those bells every morning for three hundred years, the way you hear your mother come down the stair. When the wagon went by under the branches, the oaks reached down, only a little, the way a sleeper reaches for the blanket, and each of them took a ring of sound out of the wagon and kept it. Not the bronze. The Synod could have the bronze. Just the ringing.

That is why the oaks of Oakhaven chime like a spoon on a bowl when the wind gets up. They are holding the bells for us. They keep them very quiet, because they know about the hounds too, and they let out only a little at a time, so that we will not forget what bells sounded like. And one day, the children say, when it is safe, the oaks will give the bells back all at once, and the whole town will ring the way it did on a feast morning, and nobody will be afraid of it.

A Consortium man told me last winter, quite kindly, that the oaks ring because the wood has gone soft and dense since the bore began drawing on the Root, that it is a known effect, and that it is not a good sign. I expect he is right. He is paid to be. I have kept the children's version. I notice that he did not say what will happen on the day the oaks stop.
notes: Canon: bells requisitioned for bore-teeth in the first year of the quarry, oaks chiming like a spoon on a bronze bowl since the bore, the night-hummers, hounds as a jitter in the air, the mimic rule, bound jaws and a stone on the tongue, the water-meadow and the Flume, babies humming at the crown (Book One ch. 1; Series Bible Part IV and Part VI, the Reach). The mimic learns only what is said aloud (Book One ch. 20). The last line foreshadows Vol VII (b) §2 (Ringing-Wood Day: since 18 Frostmonth 419 wood no longer rings), which the author cannot know. The jar trick echoes vox-bottles without naming them. [PROPOSED]: Margery Fallow and her school on Cooper's Row; the tales and their characters (Dorcas, Ebbo and Tilda Stint); the claim that the Reach's tales changed after the Hedge. Shelving: the Boar & Dulcimer, or the Conservatory library if Ilse Brennan keeps folk-lore.

title: Tuppence Keeps the Narrow
author: Elspeth Garland (words and pictures)
origin: Oakhaven, Cooper's Row; copied out by hand
summary: A picture-book for small children about a lamb who learns, the hard way, to keep her voice the width of a hand.
text: For the children of Cooper's Row, who have not seen a lamb this year.

Tuppence was a little lamb
with a very big voice.
BAA! said Tuppence in the morning.
BAA! said Tuppence at noon.
BAA! said Tuppence to the moon.

Hush now, said her mother, the old grey ewe.
Too loud brings the hounds, little one,
and too still brings the Hush.
We keep to the Narrow, you and I:
a hand's width of voice. No more. No less.
But Tuppence liked loud.

One evening, at the edge of the fold, she gave the biggest BAA in the world, just to see how far it would go.
It went over the wall.
It went over the hill.
It went all the way to the dark trees.
And in the dark trees, something that had been asleep lifted its head.

Tuppence saw the air at the edge of the wood go shivery, like the air over a hot stone.
She ran all the way back and pushed her nose into the old grey wool, and her mother stood very still and hummed, low and steady, until the shivery air went away.
All right, thought Tuppence. If loud is bad, I shall be quiet. I shall be the quietest lamb that ever was.

She did not baa in the morning.
She did not baa at noon.
She did not baa at the moon.
She lay down in the long grass and kept so still that the beetles walked over her hooves.

It was very quiet in the long grass.
After a while, Tuppence felt cold, though the sun was out.
After a longer while, she could not quite remember what her mother called her.
Her wool had gone pale, like the mist on the Flume.

Her mother came looking. Tuppence? Tuppence?
But a lamb who makes no sound is a hard lamb to find.

So the old grey ewe did a clever thing. She stopped calling, and she began to hum: the low, warm, middle hum, a hand's width wide. She hummed the way a hush-lamp whistles. She hummed the way the night-hummers hum at the crossings.
And Tuppence, in the long grass, heard it, and before she could think about it she hummed back.

Mmm, said Tuppence.
Not loud. Not still. Just the width of a hand.
And all at once she was warm, and her wool was her own colour again, and she remembered her name. It was Tuppence, which is what you call a small thing that is worth keeping.

That night, in the fold, by the whistling lamp, Tuppence murmured:
Goodnight, Mother.
Goodnight, lamp.
Goodnight, wall. Goodnight, hill.
Goodnight, dark trees, far away.
I am not talking to you.
And her mother laughed without making a sound, and the two of them kept the Narrow together all night long, a hand's width apart, until the morning came.
notes: Canon: the skipping rhyme 'too loud brings the hounds, too still brings the Hush' and 'murmur, my lamb, in the Narrow' (Book One ch. 1 epigraph); the hand's width of voice; hounds seen as a jitter in the air like heat-haze; the effect of falling too still: losing warmth, then name, then outline (Series Bible Part IV, the Narrow). Only the lamb's experience is shown, never the Hush. Hush-lamps and night-hummers (Book One ch. 1). The dedication agrees with the Phase 20-21 ruling that the Downs flocks were brought inside the Hedge and eaten; it hints and states nothing. [PROPOSED]: Elspeth Garland; the book itself. Suggested shelf: any Oakhaven house with children (the Cooper's Row house), or the Conservatory's children's shelf.

title: The Still Wheel at Lathbury
author: told by Kester, a miller's man of Stillwater Landing; written down by a raftsman waiting on the lock
summary: A miller's man tells what he did not find at a mill up the Flume, which is the only safe way to tell it.
text: You'll want me to tell you what was in the mill. Everyone does. I'll tell it the way my gran told hers, which is the only safe way: I'll tell you what was not there. If you want the other kind of story, there's a pedlar on the wharf who sells them by the sheet, with pictures. He has never been to Lathbury.

Lathbury Mill stands on the leat off the Flume, two miles above the lower lock, where the grown-wood channel lets a little water down to turn a wheel for the Lathbury farms. The Pargeters had it: the miller and his wife, two girls, a boy and the old mother. In the spring after the Hedge went up round Oakhaven, Lathbury stopped sending flour down to the Landing. It didn't stop all at once. The sacks came lighter, then late, then not at all. My master, Saul Ainsley, who has the mill here, was owed for a season's sacks, and on a Hearthday he took me up the towpath to ask about it. That's all it was: a man going to ask about a debt.

The first thing that was not there was the noise. You can hear Lathbury wheel from the bend below. It has a knock in the third paddle that every boatman on this water knows. We came round the bend and the wheel was turning, and there was no knock. There was no sound from the leat at all. The water came down the race white and fast and went over the wheel, as quiet as milk being poured in another house.
Saul said, Hm. That was all.

The second thing that was not there was the dog. The Pargeters kept a black bitch who barked at every raft that passed. The kennel was there, and the chain, and the collar on the end of the chain, still buckled.

The third thing was the hush-lamp. There was one in the mill-house window, and it was lit, in daylight. I could see the flame, steady, with the reed set over it the way they are, and the reed was not whistling. A lit lamp with a dumb reed over it. I have thought since that I would give a great deal to have heard that reed.

We went in, because Saul was owed. The door wasn't locked. In the kitchen the table was laid for six, and somebody had cut the bread: six slices, and the knife lying by the loaf with crumbs on it. The bread had not gone hard. That is what I could not stop looking at. It had been cut, and it had not gone hard, and there was nobody.

In the mill the stones were turning, grinding nothing, with the hopper empty. There was flour on the floor as thick as a fall of snow, and in the flour there were footprints, small ones and big ones, six people's worth. They went from the kitchen door across to the far wall. Up to the wall. Not back.
There is no door in the far wall at Lathbury. I went and looked. I put my hand on it. It was a wall.

I said to Saul, We ought to go. He said nothing. I said it again, and then I understood that I had been talking for some time, about the knock in the paddle and the bread and the wall, the way you talk when you are frightened, and he had not answered me once.

He was standing by the stones with his cap in his hands. He was there; I want to be clear about that. I could see him. But he was standing the way a man stands at a graveside, and he had not said Hm in a long while, and when I said his name it seemed to take him a moment to know it was his.

I did the only thing I knew. I hummed. It's my gran's trick, the one every child in the Reach is given with their first spoon: a hand's width, not loud, not still. I took hold of his wrist, and it was as cold as a jug from the cellar. I hummed the first thing in my head, which was a hymn, because it was Hearthday. I walked him out of that mill backwards, the two of us, keeping our eyes on the wall, and I did not stop humming until we were past the lock.

Saul Ainsley is my master still. He paid off the Pargeters' debt himself, out of his own pocket, which nobody understood, and he has never gone up the towpath again. He is a fair man and a good miller, and the Landing likes him. His wife says he was always a quiet one.

He said good morning to me today, the same as every day. I couldn't tell you how it sounded. I've lain awake trying. I have known the man eleven years and I cannot remember his voice. Nor can she, if you ask her plainly.
That's all. That's what wasn't there. If you hear me humming at the lock of a night, now you know why, and you'll do me the kindness of humming back.
notes: Told by absence only; the Hush is never named or shown (Brief; Series Bible Part IV: a person too still in siphoned country loses warmth, then name, then outline; Phase 9 parish.js uses the same technique of laid tables and a cold kettle). Canon: Stillwater Landing at the Flume's lower lock (Vol II, the Reach; js/flume16.js); the grown-wood channel; hush-lamp reeds; the hand's width; the Hedge planted in 417. The pedlar who sells tales by the sheet nods at the Cantabile serial's route upriver (Review of the Moor serial, resolution). [PROPOSED]: Lathbury Mill on a leat off the Flume, two miles above the lower lock; the Pargeter family; Kester; Saul Ainsley, miller at the Landing. Suggested library: the Bonded Store at Stillwater Landing.

title: The Lamplighter's Second Note
author: by a Lady of Cooper's Row (anonymous)
origin: Oakhaven; a fair copy passed from house to house
summary: A cooper's daughter waits all autumn for a stammering lamplighter to propose at a hand's width, and he finds another way to say it.
text: In the Reach a proposal of marriage has always been made at a hand's width: mouth to ear, so softly that nobody else could swear to the words. The orchard people said it was so the reeds would not learn it and sing it about the valley. If a third person overheard and could repeat it, it did not count, and the poor man had to begin again. My grandmother said half the weddings in Reedside were delayed a year by a sister behind a door.

It was a pretty custom when the rest of the world was loud. It is a hard one now, when everybody in Oakhaven speaks at a hand's width from morning to night. A girl cannot tell, any more, which murmurs are meant.

Mercy Hatchard could not tell. She was the cooper's daughter on Cooper's Row, twenty-four, with her father's hands and her late mother's patience. Every evening at the Listening Hour she stood at her door to watch Crispin Whitlock light the lamps.

He lit them the way other men say their prayers, one at a time and without hurrying. He put the taper up on his pole and held it to the wick, and in the moment the flame caught, before the reed above it began to whistle, he looked down at her. Then the reed found its note, thin and high, and under the cover of that note he would say something. It was never much. Cold tonight. Your father's hammer was going late. There's frost coming; I can smell it. They had eleven seconds, from the catch to the full whistle, and in a year of evenings they had spent every one of them on the weather.

Crispin had a stammer. In the old days nobody minded it. In the Narrow it was a cruelty, because a word that sticks has to be pushed, and a pushed word comes out loud. So he said short things, and he said them under the reed, and Mercy, who could have listened to him talk about frost until she was eighty, began to fear that he would never say anything else.

Her father did not fear it. Gabe Hatchard had views. He had a man in mind: Mr Osgood, a clerk at the works, who had clean cuffs, a room near the Greenhall and wages in Consortium scrip, green and black, and who came to supper on Rootdays and praised the pickled walnuts in complete sentences.

In the week the eels went down the Flume, Mr Osgood asked her. He did it properly. He leaned in at a hand's width and gave her the whole proposal in one breath, without a stumble: his prospects, his regard, a cottage with a slate roof. It was perfectly done. It was like being read a receipt.
Mercy said she would give him her answer on Nullday. Then she went upstairs and sat on her bed and did not cry, because crying carries.

On the evening before Nullday, Crispin came down Cooper's Row with his pole as usual. He lit the Bramleys' lamp, and the widow Ferrier's, and then he came to the Hatchards' and put the taper to the wick. Mercy stood at the door with her arms folded, because she had decided that if he talked about the weather tonight she would marry Mr Osgood and have done with it.
The flame caught. Crispin looked down at her and said nothing at all.

Then the reed began to whistle, and it was not her reed. He had cut a new one and set it over the lamp in the afternoon while she was at the well. It found its note, thin and high like every lamp in Oakhaven, and then, a breath later, it found another one, a little above the first. Two notes. Sweet, and wrong, and leaning on each other the way two reed-rows used to answer across a valley before the Cascade.
Every child in the Reach knows the catechism. What is holiness? One note, held without end. What is sin? The second note.

Mercy stood very still. A lamp that sang two notes could be reported, and anyone on the Row who wanted to could hear it. But nobody on the Row could have told you what it meant. It said nothing to anybody but her. He could not say it at a hand's width, so he had put it in a reed, and a reed could be overheard all it liked and nobody could repeat a word of it. By the oldest rule in the Reach, it counted.

She did not trust her voice, and in the end she did not need it. She leaned in towards the lamp, close enough to feel the heat on her cheek, and hummed the second note back, softly, at a hand's width, so that only the man on the ladder could hear.
Crispin's taper shook so badly that he dropped it, and it went out in the gutter.

Mr Osgood had his answer on Nullday, in a short note that was kinder than he expected. Gabe Hatchard came out in the morning, looked at the lamp for a long time, and said, That'll want reporting. Then he went back in to his hammer, and he never reported it. He had courted Mercy's mother in the orchards, long ago, and some people say he did it with a reed.
If you walk down Cooper's Row at the Listening Hour, among all the lamps keeping their single notes, you will hear one that does not. Nobody has reported it yet. A good many people stop to listen.
Crispin still stammers. He has never needed to say it twice.
notes: Canon: lamplighters lighting hush-lamps at dusk, each reed beginning to whistle as the lamp catches (Book One ch. 1); the catechism 'What is holiness? One note, held without end. What is sin? The second note' (Series Bible Part III); the hand's width; Consortium scrip, 'green and black' (Book One ch. 4); the Eel-Run, the night the eels go down the Flume in late Firstfruit (Vol VII (b) §2), used for the Reach way of dating by what is happening rather than by the month (Vol VII §8); Reedside and the orchards. Set in the autumn of 418, before the Church's arrival in 419. [PROPOSED]: the courtship custom of proposing at a hand's width, and the rule that an overheard proposal does not count; Mercy and Gabe Hatchard, coopers of Cooper's Row; Crispin Whitlock, lamplighter; Mr Osgood, clerk at the works; the Bramleys and the widow Ferrier, neighbours; a two-note hush-lamp reed. Suggested library: the Conservatory, or found in a house.

title: Saffery Lightfoot and the Wind That Never Stops
author: Captain Teodor Brisk, of the Fair Excuse
summary: A penny tale of the Rust Coast: a skyship captain, a Synod revenue-cutter with a brass ear, and the one wind on the Coast nobody flies into.
text: A COMPLETE TALE IN ONE NUMBER. ONE PENNY. Printed on Broadsheet Row, Port Cantabile. Not to be read aloud below decks.
They said no skyship on the Coast could outrun a revenue-cutter of the Synod. They said it mostly in taverns that Saffery Lightfoot had not yet drunk dry, and they said it to her face exactly once.

Reader, she was thirty-one years old and had been flying since she was nine. Her ship was the Patient Jenny, a lift-bellied coaster patched more often than a deacon's stockings, with two brass tanks that sang flat in cold weather and a captain who did not. Her bosun was Old Mattock, who had one eye and a great many opinions. Her lookout was the boy Fairweather, who could read a wind by licking his finger and could read nothing else.

On the night this tale begins, the Jenny was lying off the mast-tower with forty crates of moss-poultice in her hold. Every crate was untaxed, every crate was bound for Driftwood Cay, and every one was a crime. On the Cay the salvage crews work the blue jelly bare-handed, and their hands crack open in it, and the Consortium's poultice costs a sovereign a pot. Saffery had bought hers in the Reach for a tenth of that. She meant to sell it on the Cay for the same tenth. Reader, she was not a saint. She simply disliked the Consortium more than she liked money, which on this coast is very nearly the same thing.
She cast off at the dead hour with no lamps lit. Halfway across the harbour mouth, Fairweather licked his finger, held it up, and went white.
"Cutter," he whispered. "Off the Cay. Coming round."

There she was against the last of the moon: the Rectitude, revenue-cutter of the Synod, long and grey, with three tanks and a brass ear on her bow the size of a chapel door. Her listening-horn could hear a cough at a mile and a dropped spoon at two. Her commander was Grume, who had never in his life done anything that was not written down first, and who had sworn on the Synod's own paper to see Saffery Lightfoot dropped from the derrick on the Mole-head.
"Nobody breathe," said Saffery, very softly.

Nobody breathed. The Jenny ran south on the land breeze with her tanks throttled down to a murmur, and for a quarter of an hour the brass ear swung left and right like a dog's nose and found nothing. Then Fairweather sneezed.

It was not much of a sneeze. It was the smallest sneeze ever sneezed on the Rust Coast. But the brass ear swung round and stopped, and the Rectitude's tanks opened up with a roar, and she came after them like a gull after a herring.
"Well," said Old Mattock, "that's torn it."

There is only one place a ship can go on this coast where a Synod cutter will not follow, and every captain knows it, and none of them goes there. South of Cape Dissonance there is a wind that has been blowing west since the year the world went flat, and in all that time it has never once paused for breath. The fishermen call it the Endless. In the Drift, a thing set moving does not stop. A gull that flies into the Endless is never seen again. Neither is a ship.
"Mattock," said Saffery, "get out the Widow's Washing."

The Widow's Washing was a storm-kite. It was forty feet across and stitched out of every sail Saffery's mother had ever owned, and it lived rolled in the bow with a thousand fathoms of tarred line on the big winch. Saffery had never once flown it. Her mother had flown it once, long ago, and come home white-haired at forty and never said where she had been.

They put it up over the Cape with the Rectitude a quarter-mile behind and closing. For a moment it hung in the ordinary air, a great patched flag of a dead woman's sails. Then it rose into the Endless, and the line came taut with a crack like the sky breaking its knuckles, and the Patient Jenny was snatched forward so hard that Fairweather sat down on the deck.

Reader, they went. They went faster than any ship on the Coast has ever been dragged. The sea went by underneath them in a blur, and the Cape fell behind them in a single breath. Behind them the Rectitude's brass ear filled with the roar of the Endless and heard nothing else at all. A cough at a mile, a spoon at two, but not a ship inside the loudest wind in the world.
Commander Grume consulted his regulations. His regulations said that no vessel of the Synod was to enter the Endless. He turned for home, and he wrote it down.

So the Jenny was free. And the Jenny was going west at a speed no ship can live at, behind a kite in a wind that would never stop, towards an edge of the world nobody has charted, and the big winch began to smoke.
"Cut it," said Mattock.
Saffery looked up at her mother's sails, high and small and pulling. She thought of her mother at forty with her white hair, saying nothing. She took out her mother's knife.
"Captain," said Fairweather, "will it come down?"
"No," said Saffery. "Not ever. Not in the Drift." And she cut the line herself.

The Jenny fell out of the Endless like a stone out of a sling and came down into ordinary air above an ordinary sea, slow and quiet and very surprised. They coasted to Driftwood Cay on what was left of the land breeze and sold forty crates of poultice for a tenth of a sovereign a pot. On the Cay, a man with a cracked hand shook Saffery's, and it was the best price she ever got.

Fishermen off the Cape say that on a clear evening you can still see it, very high and very small, going west, and going faster. In the Drift, nothing that is let go of ever stops. Saffery Lightfoot knew that when she cut it.
Reader, she cut it anyway.
notes: In-world pulp; its excesses are the author's, not canon. Canon: Broadsheet Row as the only free press (Vol I §III, the Archipelago; Vol II; game's Cantabile serial); the mast-tower, the Long Mole and the derrick and the drop (Vol IV, the Rust Coast; Series Bible Part X-B); Driftwood Cay, where dissolved hulls come ashore as blue jelly (Vol II); the Drift's winds that never stop, and set things moving that do not stop (Series Bible Part IV law-rot and Part VI, Tempest Archipelago); Cape Dissonance; the year the world went flat (412); listening-horns on Synod hunting vessels (Book One ch. 21, the Office cutter; Vol VI §6.3); lift-tanks; moss-poultice (Vol II, Rowena Pell's Resonant Moss Poultice); sovereigns. The Kestrel's crew is a likely readership; Vane would not read it, being off the sea. [PROPOSED]: Teodor Brisk; Saffery Lightfoot, the Patient Jenny, Old Mattock, Fairweather; the Synod revenue-cutter Rectitude and Commander Grume; the Endless, a never-ending wind south of Cape Dissonance; the Widow's Washing storm-kite; the price of poultice. The cutter is called a revenue-cutter to keep it apart from the Office cutter of Book One. Suggested library: the Bonded Store at Stillwater (a Cantabile print come upriver), or found below decks on the Drift-Kestrel.

title: Under a Hand's Width
author: Edwy Marchbank, formerly reed-pruner of the Reedside orchards
summary: Nine short poems by an old orchard pruner, from the last singing summer to a child born quiet and brought round.
text: I pruned reeds in the orchards for thirty-one years. Now I sweep the Chapel. These are short, because everything is. Whoever finds this in the pew: it is yours. Read it under your breath.

I. PRUNING
You cut a reed to make it sing.
Too long, it mumbles. Too short, it shrieks.
My master put the knife in my hand at nine
and said, Listen first. Cut after.
Thirty-one years I listened first.
I should like that written on me somewhere.

II. THE HOUR OF SUGAR
The reeds went clear as barley-sugar
in the time it takes to say a grace,
and then the wind came down off the hill
the way it always had, meaning no harm,
and I watched thirty-one years of listening
blow over Greenroot like a fine snow.

III. FLAT
My wife says the reds have gone.
I say the reds are the same; it is our eyes.
We have had this argument for six autumns.
Neither of us has once said the other thing:
that we would both give a great deal
to be wrong.

IV. THE BELLS
They took the bells on a Massday.
Nobody rang them going.
That was the worst of it, I think:
not that they went, but that we let them
leave the town as quiet as stolen spoons.

V. WOOL
We planted the Hedge with our own hands
and packed it with our own fleece,
and every cough in Oakhaven goes into it now
and stays. I think of them some nights:
all those coughs, all those dropped pans,
all those children told to hush,
kept in the wool like letters never sent.
I hope it is a kind keeper.
I know what it is keeping them from.

VI. NIGHT-HUMMER
Old women on stools at the crossings,
humming nothing in particular
so that the street will not go quiet.
I used to think the Cantors held the Reach together.
It was these. It was always these.

VII. THE OAKS
Since the bore, the oaks ring when the wind moves:
a spoon on a bowl, a bell in the next valley.
The children think it lovely.
I pruned for sound all my life, and I know
what a thing sounds like when it has been
pulled too tight.

VIII. INSTRUCTIONS FOR MY BURYING
Bind my jaw. Fine. Put the stone on my tongue.
I have said what I meant to.
But leave my hands loose, Hannah,
in case there is pruning.

IX. FOR A CHILD BORN QUIET, WHO WAS BROUGHT ROUND
You came out without a sound,
and the whole room held its breath with you,
and then the Cantor hummed into the top of your head
and you creased your face up like a walnut
and made a noise the width of a hand.
Nobody cheered. We have forgotten how.
But I want you to know, small one,
that an old man in the next house,
who used to tune the orchards,
heard you through the wall,
and stood up,
and took off his cap.
notes: Canon: the wind-reed orchards tuned by pruning, audible from Greenroot, which turned to sugar-glass and blew away on the day of the Fracture (Book One ch. 1; Series Bible Part VI, the Reach); the paler reds 'everyone over thirty' notices (Book One ch. 1; Series Bible Part III); the bells requisitioned for bore-teeth; the Hedge packed with wool (Book One ch. 1; Phase 20-21 ruling); the oaks ringing since the bore (Book One ch. 1); night-hummers; bound jaws and a stone on the tongue; births hummed at the crown and the 'still ones' (Book One ch. 1). Poem V's 'kept in the wool' follows Vol V's ruling as cited in Phase 13 (the Hedge keeps every sound Oakhaven made) without stating it. Poem IX describes a birth like Ruth Madder's but names no one and is dated 418. Massday for the bells is not attested. [PROPOSED]: Edwy Marchbank and his wife Hannah; Edwy sweeping the Chapel; the bells taken on a Massday. Suggested library: the Conservatory, or left in a Chapel pew.

title: The Bellwether Book: Songs Writ In Behind the Bar
author: kept by Reuben Thrale, landlord, and the drovers who stopped; last entry by G. Thrale
summary: The drovers' inn's songbook, written in by many hands over forty years, until the night the house was shut.
text: Rule of the house. Any drover who sings a song in this house that is not in this book shall write it in, or buy the room a jug. Spelling no object. R. Thrale.

THE DROVE-ROAD
(Every man knows it. Written in so the boys get the verses in the right order.)
Over the Long Down and down by the thorn,
eight hundred ewes and a tup with a horn,
bell at his throat and the dogs at his heel,
drive 'em to Oakhaven, home for a meal.
Walk on, walk on, it's only a mile
to the Bellwether's fire at the foot of the stile.

(The second verse is ruder. You know it. A. L.)
(He means he don't know it. R. T.)

FOLD-FIRE
(For the back-end of the year, when the beacons are lit.)
Long Down burning, north and high,
Hob's Knap answers from the eastern sky,
Ewe Barrow west on the old long mound:
come down, my flock, come down, come down.
Come down to the light, come down to the fold,
the night is long and the hill is cold.
(Sung at the window while Absalom goes up and lights them. He cannot sing. He lights them anyway. R. T.)

SCOURING THE RAM
(For the seventh summer. Sung on the scarp, one verse to a stake.)
Chalk him white and cut him clean,
the whitest Ram that ever was seen;
scour him once in seven year
or he'll walk off the hill and the flock with him, dear.
Scoured 395. Scoured 402. Scoured 409, rain all week, and the Farrant girl fell in the trench and came up white as the Ram. R. T.

THE SHEAF SONG
(Oakhaven's way. Wethercombe cuts its own last stand to it. One cut to a beat, and never one man alone.)
Cut it low, and cut it slow,
the last of the year is let to go.
(That's all there is of it, and all there needs to be. You sing it round till the stand's down. R. T.)

THE MILLER'S DAUGHTER
Not written. Both verses. If you need it written down, you are too young to hear it. R. T.

A NOTE, IN THE SAME HAND, LATER AND SMALLER
Since the year the reds went, a song carried over the Downs brings what we do not name in this house. Sing them low now. Any man who sings full voice outside this door buys nobody a jug, because he will not be here to. R. T., 413.

THE LOW SONG
(Made in this house the winter of 414, for the Narrow, by all of us, but mostly by Cicely from the fold.)
Low, low, the width of a hand,
lambs in the fold and the ewes on the land;
not loud for the hounds and not still for the other,
low, low, as you'd hum to your mother.
Low, low, and the lamp on the sill,
somebody's humming on every hill.
(Best sung by three or four, so there's always one breathing in while another breathes out. That way it never stops. A. L.)
My nephew Gideon has the house from Reed-Hanging. My chest will not do the stairs, and the house wants a pair of legs. Keep the book, boy. Make them write in. R. T., 416.
416, high summer. Nobody went up to scour the Ram. Next year, we said. G. T.

417, back-end. Shut tonight. The wool has gone down to Oakhaven for the Hedge, and the flocks with it, and we are all to go in behind it: Tamar and all the Farrants, the fold, me. The road is empty. I sang the Drove-Road on the doorstep, low, the way Uncle said, to nobody.
I am leaving the book on the bar for whoever opens the door next. If it is me, I will know the songs. If it is not, learn the low one first.
G. Thrale.
notes: Canon: the Bellwether, Wethercombe's drovers' inn, shut by Gideon Thrale the night the Hedge closed and reopened when Tamar came back; Gideon 'had it from my uncle'; eight hundred sheep a fair-day; the fold-fires on the Long Down, Hob's Knap and Ewe Barrow, lit by Absalom Rudd 'forty back-ends running'; the Chalk Ram, which must be scoured every seven years or it walks off the hill with the flock, 'grown over for ten years' by 419 (Phase 22 in-game text). The flocks driven down for the Hedge's wool and kept inside it (Phase 20-21 Author Rulings). The Sheaf Song's couplet (Phase 12 in-game text, js/festivals12.js; still marked [PROPOSED] there); the Miller's Daughter, 'both verses', the rude one (Phase 9 in-game text; js/companion-talk.js), whose words are deliberately not given. Hounds brought by song since 412 (Series Bible Part IV, the World Went Flat). Reed-Hanging (Vol VII (b) §2). [PROPOSED]: Reuben Thrale as Gideon's uncle's name and the book's keeper; the drover A. L.; Cicely from the fold; the words of the Drove-Road, Fold-Fire, Scouring the Ram and the Low Song; the scouring years 395, 402 and 409; a Farrant girl in 409. Kept at the Bellwether, where it belongs; it could be read there or bought from Gideon.

title: The Last Sheaf: A Harvest Play in Three Scenes
author: as played at the edge of the north field, Harvest Home 418; set down by Ursula Dimmock for next year's players
summary: The old harvest play as Oakhaven now plays it: a reaper who cannot cut alone, a voice at the gate nobody may answer, and a sheaf that asks to be let end.
text: A NOTE FOR PLAYERS. The play is older than anyone in Oakhaven. In my mother's day the third part was the Thief of Bread, and the whole field shouted him off. You cannot shout anybody off now, so since the Hedge the Thief has become the Voice at the Gate. He is not shouted off. He is not answered. It works better, I think. It is certainly more frightening.

It is played at the edge of the field by lamplight, at a hand's width, so the watchers must come close. Nobody, player or watcher, is to answer the Voice. Whoever answers brings the cider next year. The Voice may say anything it likes to the crowd except the true name of somebody dead. We are not cruel, only careful.

THE PLAYERS
THE SHEAF, a child in a straw coat, who stands in the last stand and says nothing until the end.
OLD REAPER, with a wooden sickle.
THE BINDER, his wife, who has the sense.
THE VOICE AT THE GATE, never seen; played from behind a hung fleece by whoever has the best ear for other people.
THE VILLAGE, which is everybody else.

SCENE ONE. THE FIELD. Evening.
(REAPER comes on with his sickle and finds THE SHEAF standing very still in the stand.)
REAPER. There she is. Last of the year. I'll have her down before supper.
BINDER. You'll not. Not on your own.
REAPER. I've cut the whole field on my own.
BINDER. And it grew back by morning, every stalk of it, and the bread tastes of less each time.
REAPER. Bread's bread.
BINDER. Bread was bread.
(REAPER swings at THE SHEAF. THE SHEAF does not fall. He swings again. THE SHEAF folds its arms.)
REAPER. She's a stubborn one.
BINDER. The last stand is never cut by one. Everybody knows that.
REAPER. Then fetch everybody.
BINDER. (turning to the watchers) Everybody's here. Look at them, standing about with their hands in their shawls.
REAPER. They'll want feeding first.
BINDER. They always do.

SCENE TWO. THE GATE. Night.
(The fleece is the Hedge. REAPER and BINDER sit with their backs to it, eating. THE SHEAF stands where it stood.)
VOICE. (behind the fleece, in an old woman's voice) Son? Son, come out to the gate. I've brought your supper, and it's hot.
REAPER. (half rising) Mam?
BINDER. (her hand over his mouth) Your mam's been a year in the churchyard with a stone on her tongue. Sit down.
VOICE. (in the BINDER's own voice, exactly) Husband, leave her. Come out. I'm out here. That's not me in there with you.
(REAPER looks from the fleece to his wife, and back.)
REAPER. (muffled) Which of you is it?
BINDER. Which of us has her hand over your mouth?
(REAPER thinks about this, and sits down.)
VOICE. (to the watchers) You there, in the blue shawl. Your boy's out here. He says he's cold. Won't you say something to him? Only a word.
(Here the watchers say nothing, and the Voice goes along the crowd, coaxing, for as long as the player can bear it. The Voice must never be answered. If it is, the play stops, the one who answered is told what they owe, and we begin the scene again.)
VOICE. (at last, softly) Nobody? Nobody at all?
BINDER. Not tonight, thank you.

SCENE THREE. THE CUT. Before dawn.
(THE VILLAGE comes forward round THE SHEAF, all of it, as many as there are. Everybody who has a blade holds it up, and everybody who has none holds up a finger. The tune is hummed, low, sixteen beats, and on every beat every hand makes one cut in the air.)
ALL. (under the breath) Cut it low, and cut it slow, the last of the year is let to go.
(On the sixteenth beat THE SHEAF kneels down. Then, for the first time, it speaks.)
THE SHEAF. Thank you. I was so tired of growing back.
REAPER. Will you grow back tomorrow?
THE SHEAF. No. Not this one. This one you let end.
(THE SHEAF stands up out of its straw coat, and is only a child again. BINDER plaits the coat into the sheaf-figure, and the whole field carries it to the Hedge-gate and hangs it there till spring.)
VOICE. (behind the fleece)
(The Voice says nothing more. It has nothing to say to people who are all together. That is the end of the play.)

AFTERWARDS. Nobody claps, because clapping carries. The players hum the tune once more through, and the child who was the Sheaf is given the first slice of the hearth bread and goes home asleep in somebody's arms. This year Hodge Lorkin answered the Voice in Scene Two, because it did his father very well. He has promised the cider for next year without being asked. U. D.
notes: Canon: the Last Sheaf, cut by the whole village singing the Sheaf Song in unison, a cut on every beat, the one sheaf allowed to stay cut as a promise that things are allowed to end, the sheaf-figure hung on the Hedge-gate till spring, hearth bread (Vol VII (b) §2); the grain that regrows within a day and tastes of less (Vol VII (b) §2, citing Vol I); the sixteen-beat tune and its couplet (Phase 12 in-game text, js/festivals12.js, still [PROPOSED] there); the mimic rule and voices at the Hedge (Series Bible Part IV; Book One ch. 1); a stone on the tongue of the dead. The Voice going silent before people who are together agrees with the Wearer luring the lone listener (Book One ch. 1, 6). Dated Harvest Home 418, before the 419 postponement. [PROPOSED]: the play, its history (the Thief of Bread), its rules and forfeit; Ursula Dimmock; Hodge Lorkin. Shelved at the watchhouse, by the Hedge-gate where the sheaf hangs; the Conservatory would also keep a copy. Check 'Hodge Lorkin' and 'Dimmock' against new names from the other writers.

title: The Eight Keepers, and the Sparrow Who Asked
author: Constance Farthing, who taught the small voices their letters
summary: Nine bedtime fables for a children's choir: eight animals who each keep one thing in the world, and a sparrow with no job at all.
text: For the small voices of the charitable choir, Cloister road. These are told one a night before hymn practice, and on the ninth night the Sparrow. They are very old and I have not improved them, except to take out a bear, who frightened the youngest.

THE BADGER WHO KEPT THE ROOTS
In the beginning everything grew every which way: up and down, and sideways into next week. So the Badger went under the ground and told every root, one at a time, which way was down. He is telling them still. If you put your ear to the earth in spring you will hear a sort of humming. That is the Badger going round, saying down, and down, and down.
Moral: somebody has to say it every time.

THE SALAMANDER WHO KEPT THE HEARTH
Fire did not used to know its own size. A candle might burn down a barn, and a bonfire might not warm a cup. So the Salamander sat in the middle of every flame and told it how big to be: the size of a hand for a hand, the size of a house only for a house.
Moral: mind the size of things.

THE TORTOISE WHO KEPT THE WEIGHT
When you put down a cup, it stays where you put it. That is because the Tortoise is holding it down for you, and holding down the table, and the house, and the hill the house stands on. It is slow work, and he does not complain.
Moral: say thank you to your cup.

THE HERON WHO KEPT THE HOURS
The Heron stands in the river of the hours and does not move, so that the hours can go past him in their proper order, one and then the next. If he ever stepped out, they would all pile up against each other like logs at a weir, and next Nullday would happen on top of breakfast.
Moral: stand still when it is your turn to stand still.

THE COCKEREL WHO KEPT THE MORNING
Every day the Cockerel calls the light up over the edge of the world, and every day it comes. Nobody has ever thanked him, because he is noisy.
Moral: a thing can be useful and still be annoying. This is true of choirs.

THE HARE WHO KEPT THINGS GOING
The wind, the rivers, a ball thrown in the yard: they all go because the Hare keeps them going, and she never sits down to do it. That is why you cannot catch a hare.
Moral: do not try. She is busy.

THE MAGPIE WHO KEPT WHAT WAS REMEMBERED
The Magpie loves bright things, and the brightest things of all are the things we remember: the way to your gran's door, the words of the third verse, the names of everybody you love. She keeps them in her nest so that nobody loses them for good.
Moral: if you forget something, it is not gone. The Magpie has it. Ask her nicely.

THE OWL WHO KEPT THE RESTS
Between every note of every song there is a little rest, and the Owl keeps those. A rest sounds like nothing, but it is not nothing. It is our nothing: the good quiet, the quiet of a house asleep. Outside the edge of the world there is another quiet, which belongs to nobody, and it would very much like to come in. It cannot get past the Owl. She keeps all the gaps filled with our own quiet, the way you fill a doorway by standing in it.
Moral: not all quiet is the same quiet.

THE SPARROW WHO ASKED
The Hedge-sparrow was very small and had no job at all. She went to each of the Keepers in turn and asked: When do you sleep?
The Badger said, When somebody comes to say down for me.

The Salamander said the same, and so did the Tortoise. The Heron said it without moving his beak. The Cockerel said it loudly. The Hare said it running past. The Magpie said it and then forgot she had, and the Owl said it very softly, in a rest.
Who is coming? asked the Sparrow.
We were told that somebody would, said the Owl. It was a long time ago.
The Sparrow thought about this for a whole afternoon, which is a long time for a sparrow. Then she went back under the ground to the Badger and said, Show me how you say down.
And the Badger laughed, which nobody had ever heard him do before, and began to teach her.
Moral: little ones should make themselves useful. That is what I tell the choir, at any rate. The children have decided it means something else, and they will not tell me what.
notes: Written before 412 and 416, so the author knows nothing of the Fracture or the Forgetting; the Cockerel and the Magpie read with hard irony for a player who finds the book in the empty Cloister. Canon: the eight laws, Growth, Heat, Mass, Time, Light, Velocity, Memory, Decay (Series Bible Part III); Decay as 'the rest between notes, the silence that belongs to the world, which keeps out the silence that belongs to nothing' (Part III, the Gate of Decay); the lost curriculum surviving as folk-craft (Part III). The fables state nothing as fact. They are a garbled folk memory that the author misreads, in line with the Brief's rule that an in-world author may only rumour or be wrong. The Sparrow fable deliberately echoes the Compact (Part III) and the canonical ending's teaching of the law-songs (Part X) without naming Choristers, Spires or relief. If that is too near the central secret, cut the Owl's line 'We were told that somebody would'. The Cloister was a charitable choir on the Cloister road whose old name nobody remembers (Book One ch. 17 epigraph and opening), so the book does not give it. [PROPOSED]: Constance Farthing; the book; the eight beast-keepers. The octave-week is used in the Heron fable (Series Bible Part I). Suggested library: the Moot-house in Whisper-Grove, or found in the Cloister choir-room.

title: Hand on It: A Tale of the Eleventh, in Four Counts
author: Magda Rusch, of no House
origin: Cinderhold, Tier Eleven; a Bellows chapbook, carried west by a Deep Guild fitter
summary: A deaf old striker, the granddaughter who swore to be his ears, and the day the Great Beat missed a fall.
text: This is told the Eleventh way. Three counts of story, and then the fall, when you shut your mouth. Where it says Fall, wait for it.

Kolb struck plate on the Eleventh for forty years. He swung the bar. He kept the count.
Fall.

He could not hear the Beat any more. Forty years of it had taken his ears. He felt it in his boots instead.
Fall.

His granddaughter Grete carried water to the crew. She was eleven, and of no House. She talked between the falls, like everybody.
Fall.

The crew had a word for Kolb now. They said it between the falls, behind his back, though he could not have heard it to his face. The word was cold.
Fall.

It was the whistle. On the Eleventh everybody listens for it. A pipe that has run cool for a week remembers all at once, and before it remembers it sings, high and thin, F-sharp. Then you have four counts to get behind basalt. Mouth open. Eyes shut.
Fall.

A deaf man does not hear the whistle. A deaf man on a crew stands there while it sings. And whoever goes back for him is the second man burned.
Fall.

The foreman, Ruprecht, said it to Grete's face, because he could not say it to Kolb's ears. Your grandda's off the crew at end of shift. I'm sorry for it.
Fall.

Grete said: I'll be his ears.
Fall.

Ruprecht laughed. A child for ears, on the striking floor. Then he saw she meant it, and stopped laughing, and said: Who'll swear for that?
Fall.

Kolb had read every word off their mouths. He went to the furnace mouth. He took the ingot out bare-handed and held it.
Fall.

He held it through a whole count of four, with the crew watching and the smell going up, and he said: She's my ears. Hand on it.
Fall.

Nobody called him cold after that.
Fall.

So it went. Grete at his elbow, with the water and with her hand on his wrist. They had a sign between them. For the whistle: the flat of her hand, hard, once. Then you run.
Fall.

It went that way all spring and all summer. Twice the whistle came. Twice the flat of her hand came down on his wrist, and twice old Kolb was behind the basalt before the younger men.
Fall.

Then, on a Driftday at the back end of the year, the Great Beat missed.
Not stopped. Nobody alive has heard it stop. It missed one fall, the way your heart does when you miss a stair in the dark.
And there was no
There was no fall.

Every soul on the Eleventh froze where they stood. Mid-word, mid-swing, mid-breath. A body raised under the Beat does not know what to do in the gap where a fall should be. It holds you like a hand. Four counts. Sometimes more.
And in the gap, high and thin, a pipe began to sing.
Grete heard it. Grete was frozen with the rest, with her mouth open on a word and her hand on her grandda's wrist, and the hand would not come down.
Kolb did not hear the whistle. Kolb had not heard the Beat in eleven years. There was nothing missing in his ears, because there had been nothing in them to miss.
He looked at the crew standing like a row of nails. He looked at the child at his elbow with her mouth open. He looked where she was looking.
He picked Grete up under one arm. He took Ruprecht by the collar with the other hand. And he walked behind the basalt like a man going home for his supper.

One.
Two.
Three.
And the pipe remembered.
Fall.

The Beat came back. It always does. Five of the crew were burned, and they lived. Ruprecht has a scar from his ear to his collarbone, and on the Eleventh that is a rank, and he wears it like one. Nobody died. On the Eleventh, that is worth a date.
Fall.

Ruprecht came to Kolb after and said it between the falls, loud, so the whole crew heard: He kept his hand on it. There is nothing higher you can say of anybody in Cinderhold.
Fall.

Kolb could not hear it. He looked at Grete. She took his wrist and tapped it out with her fingers, four little taps, one to a count.
Fall.

That is what four taps on the wrist mean on the Eleventh now. Not the whistle; the whistle is still the flat of the hand. Four taps with the fingers mean: he kept his hand on it.
Fall.
Tell it between the falls. It is short on purpose.
notes: Canon: Cinderhold's four-beat industrial pulse, speech between hammer-falls (Vol I §III.3; Vol II, Cinderhold); the Great Beat, which has stopped only twice in two hundred years, and beat-drift, in which every Cinderholder in earshot freezes mid-word when it skips (Vol II, Cinderhold, hazard 4); the F-sharp whistle, four seconds to basalt, 'dive behind basalt, mouth open, eyes shut', and the pipe that 'remembered' after a week cool (Vol I §III.3, the Tier Three disaster of 417); the bare-handed ingot oath, 'cold' meaning cowardly, and 'he kept his hand on it' as the highest praise (Vol I §III.3; Vol II dialect); Tier Eleven, of no House; the Bellows, Tier Eleven's union (Vol II). Struck, not sung, music (Vol I). The Moor serial's resolution set the precedent that Cinderhold texts use the Beat instead of the Narrow. The burns are not described, and the child is not hurt. [PROPOSED]: Magda Rusch; Kolb, Grete and the foreman Ruprecht; the four-tap sign; the Bellows printing chapbooks; a Deep Guild fitter carrying it to the Oakhaven works. No Furnace House is named. Suggested shelf: the quarry or Depot Three (a fitter's chapbook), or the Bonded Store at Stillwater.
